newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan to raise water prices to cut waste.
newsitem.headline: Jordan to raise water prices to cut waste.

text.p: Jordan said on Tuesday it was raising water prices from next October for upper-income consumers as part of IMF-directed free market reforms to cut waste and raise funds to improve services.

Water Ministry officials said the tariff rise to take effect at the start of October will help raise an extra 20 million dinars ($28 million) for the state, offset rising running costs and improve services.
But even with the coming price hike, the second in nearly a year, the government will still be selling water to household consumers at below cost, officials said.

The new rates nearly double the bill for a 20 percent segment of upper-income consumers who use large quantities of water and provide 60 percent of total government revenues for water supplied by the state, officials said.
But it should not affect the majority of low-income consumers who could see charges going down, officials said.

"Nearly sixty percent of consumers will not be affected by the raise in tariffs and they are the group which consume small quantities of water," Water Minister Munzir Haddadin told reporters after a cabinet meeting which approved the decision.
"It will only affect those who consume large quantities of water," said Haddadin adding he hoped higher prices will cut waste in the parched kingdom.
Residents of the capital Amman receive water only a few times a week through the long hot summer, part of rationing of scarce supplies by a country which suffers from a chronic water shortage.

The International Monetary Fund, which oversees the kingdom's structural economic reforms, has advised the government to streamline its subsidy of essential services to ease a chronic budget deficit and remove distortions in its aid-dependent economy.

The government is however acutely aware of the risks of a complete elimination of subsidies on bread and on basic services, which is an explosive issue in a country where poverty and unemployment are on the rise. -- Amman Newsroom +9626-623776
